vjimc-2009-cat1-01.title: Halving the base angles
vjimc-2009-cat1-01.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle CAB$, $\beta=\angle CBA$ and let $\alpha_n,\beta_n$ be the angles of triangle $ABC_n$ at $A$ and $B$. The incenter $C_{n+1}$ lies inside triangle $ABC_n$ on the bisectors of its angles at $A$ and $B$, so $C_{n+1}$ is on the same side of $AB$ as $C$ and
$$\alpha_{n+1}=\frac{\alpha_n}2,\quad\beta_{n+1}=\frac{\beta_n}2,\qquad\text{hence}\quad \alpha_n=\frac{\alpha}{2^n},\ \beta_n=\frac{\beta}{2^n}.$$

Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(c,0)$ and $C_n=(x_n,y_n)$ with $y_n>0$. For $n\ge1$ both $\alpha_n,\beta_n$ are acute, so $0<x_n<c$ and
$$\tan\alpha_n=\frac{y_n}{x_n},\qquad\tan\beta_n=\frac{y_n}{c-x_n}.$$
Eliminating $y_n$: $x_n\tan\alpha_n=(c-x_n)\tan\beta_n$, so
$$x_n=\frac{c\tan\beta_n}{\tan\alpha_n+\tan\beta_n},\qquad y_n=x_n\tan\alpha_n .$$
Since $\tan(\theta/2^n)=\frac\theta{2^n}(1+o(1))$,
$$x_n=\frac{c\,\beta\,(1+o(1))}{\alpha(1+o(1))+\beta(1+o(1))}\longrightarrow\frac{c\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\qquad y_n\le c\tan\alpha_n\to0 .$$
Hence $C_n$ converges to the point $L$ of segment $AB$ with
$$AL=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\,AB,\qquad LB=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,AB,$$
i.e. $AL:LB=\beta:\alpha$ and $L=\frac{\alpha A+\beta B}{\alpha+\beta}$ (the larger the angle at a vertex, the closer $L$ is to that vertex). A numerical iteration confirms this. ∎

vjimc-2009-cat1-02.title: Divisibility by 3 or by a Fermat number
vjimc-2009-cat1-02.body:
Let $M=2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1$ with $k\ge3$.

**$k$ even.** Then $2^k-1$ is odd, so $2^{2^k-1}\equiv2\pmod 3$, and $2^k\equiv1\pmod3$. Thus $M\equiv2-1-1=0\pmod3$, and $M>3$, so $M$ is composite.

**$k$ odd.** Let $F_j=2^{2^j}+1$. From $(2^{2^j}-1)(2^{2^j}+1)=2^{2^{j+1}}-1$ we get by induction
$$2^{2^k}-1=F_0F_1\cdots F_{k-1}.$$
Also
$$2M=2^{2^k}-2^{k+1}-2=\left(2^{2^k}-1\right)-\left(2^{k+1}+1\right).$$
Since $k+1$ is even, write $k+1=2^aq$ with $a\ge1$ and $q$ odd. As $y+1\mid y^q+1$ for odd $q$, with $y=2^{2^a}$,
$$F_a=2^{2^a}+1\ \Big|\ 2^{2^aq}+1=2^{k+1}+1 .$$
Moreover $2^a\le k+1\le2^{k-1}$ for $k\ge3$, so $a\le k-1$ and $F_a$ is one of the factors of $2^{2^k}-1$. Therefore $F_a\mid 2M$, and since $F_a$ is odd, $F_a\mid M$.

Finally $1<F_a\le2^{k+1}+1<M$: indeed for $k\ge3$ we have $2^k-1\ge k+3$, so $M-(2^{k+1}+1)=2^{2^k-1}-3\cdot2^k-2\ge 8\cdot2^k-3\cdot2^k-2>0$. Hence $M$ has a proper divisor and is composite. (E.g. $k=3$: $M=119=7\cdot17$ with $F_2=17$; $k=5$: $F_1=5\mid M$.) ∎

vjimc-2009-cat1-03.title: A homogeneous linear system
vjimc-2009-cat1-03.body:
Consider the system of $k$ homogeneous linear equations in the $n$ real unknowns $x_1,\dots,x_n$:
$$\sum_{j\in A_i}x_j=0,\qquad i=1,\dots,k .$$
Since $k<n$, it has a nontrivial solution (the solution space has dimension at least $n-k\ge1$). Colour $j$ red if $x_j>0$, blue if $x_j<0$, and leave it uncoloured if $x_j=0$.

- Condition (i) holds by construction, and (ii) because some $x_j\ne0$.
- For (iii), suppose $A_i$ contains a coloured element, say a red one $j$ ($x_j>0$). As $\sum_{l\in A_i}x_l=0$, some $l\in A_i$ has $x_l<0$, i.e. is blue. Similarly a blue element forces a red one. So $A_i$ is either entirely uncoloured or contains both colours. ∎

vjimc-2009-cat1-04.title: Gaps for positive sequences; cancelling blocks for real ones
vjimc-2009-cat1-04.body:
**(a) No.** Let $a_i>0$ and suppose the sequence covers $\mathbb N$. Let $G_k=\sum_ia_i^k\in(0,\infty]$ and let $k_0$ be the least $k$ with $G_k<\infty$ (it exists, since some $G_k$ equals $1$). Then $a_i\to0$, so $T=\{i:a_i>1\}$ is finite, and for $k\ge k_0$,
$$\sum_{i\notin T}a_i^k\le\sum_{i\notin T}a_i^{k_0}\le G_{k_0}=:C,$$
because $0<a_i\le1$ for $i\notin T$. So the finite values of $G$ are exactly $G_k$, $k\ge k_0$.

If $T=\emptyset$, then $G_k\le C$ for all $k\ge k_0$, so large integers are not attained. Otherwise let $M=\max_ia_i>1$, attained by $r\ge1$ indices, let $t=|T|$ and $\Lambda=\max\big(\{1\}\cup\{a_i: i\in T,\ a_i<M\}\big)<M$. For $k\ge k_0$,
$$rM^k\le G_k\le U_k:=rM^k+t\Lambda^k+C ,$$
and $U_k$ increases with $k$. Since $\frac{rM^{k+1}-U_k}{M^k}=r(M-1)-t\left(\frac{\Lambda}M\right)^k-\frac C{M^k}\to r(M-1)>0$, we have $rM^{k+1}-U_k\to\infty$; choose $k_1\ge k_0$ with $rM^{k_1+1}-U_{k_1}>2$ and an integer $Z$ with $U_{k_1}<Z<rM^{k_1+1}$. For $k_0\le k\le k_1$: $G_k\le U_k\le U_{k_1}<Z$; for $k>k_1$: $G_k\ge rM^k>Z$. So $Z$ is not covered — a contradiction.

**(b) Yes.** Write $S_m(x)=\sum_ix_i^{2m+1}$ for a finite sequence $x$.

*Lemma.* For every $n\ge0$ there is a finite sequence $x^{(n)}$ of length $3^n$ with entries in $[-1,1]$, $S_m(x^{(n)})=0$ for $0\le m<n$ and $S_m(x^{(n)})\neq0$ for $m\ge n$.
*Proof by induction.* $x^{(0)}=(1)$. Given $x=x^{(n)}$, let $\lambda=2^{-1/(2n+1)}$ and let $y$ be the concatenation $(-x,\lambda x,\lambda x)$. Then $S_m(y)=\left(2\lambda^{2m+1}-1\right)S_m(x)$. For $m<n$ this is $0$; for $m=n$, $2\lambda^{2n+1}-1=0$; for $m>n$, $\lambda^{2m+1}=2^{-(2m+1)/(2n+1)}<\frac12$, so the factor is nonzero. Entries stay in $[-1,1]$. $\square$

*Construction.* Start with $F_0=(1)$, so $S_0(F_0)=1$. For $j\ge1$, given a finite sequence $F_{j-1}$ with $S_m(F_{j-1})=m+1$ for $0\le m\le j-1$, let $c_j=j+1-S_j(F_{j-1})$, $d_j=S_j(x^{(j)})\ne0$, choose an integer $N_j\ge1$ so large that
$$\lambda_j=\left(\frac{c_j}{N_jd_j}\right)^{1/(2j+1)}\quad\text{(real odd root) satisfies}\quad|\lambda_j|\le\frac{3^{-j}}{j},$$
and let $F_j$ be $F_{j-1}$ followed by $N_j$ copies of $\lambda_jx^{(j)}$. Since $S_m(\lambda x^{(j)})=\lambda^{2m+1}S_m(x^{(j)})$, the sums $S_m$ for $m<j$ do not change, and $S_j(F_j)=S_j(F_{j-1})+N_j\lambda_j^{2j+1}d_j=j+1$. Let $(a_i)$ be the infinite sequence that extends all $F_j$.

*Convergence.* Fix $m\ge0$ and consider a partial sum $P_L=\sum_{i\le L}a_i^{2m+1}$ with $L$ beyond the end of $F_m$. The first $L$ terms are $F_{j-1}$ for some $j>m$, then some complete copies of $\lambda_jx^{(j)}$ (each contributing $0$ because $m<j$), then part of one more copy, which contributes at most $3^j|\lambda_j|^{2m+1}\le3^j|\lambda_j|\le\frac1j$ in absolute value. Hence $|P_L-(m+1)|\le\frac1j$, and $j\to\infty$ as $L\to\infty$. So
$$\sum_{i=1}^\infty a_i^{2m+1}=m+1\qquad(m=0,1,2,\dots),$$
and every positive integer $M$ is obtained with $k=2M-1$.

**Answer: (a) No; (b) Yes.** ∎
